composition_models.NEW-U08-READING-01: Three men and one ship are on the shore. A certain man says: “Who is the man who has that ship?” His companion says: “The man is my companion. He has the fish that we see.” “To whom do you give the fish?” “I give it to the man who helped me.” “Which ship does he have?” “He has the little ship that you saw.”

task_models.analysis_targets: How does the man swim? asks manner; Why does the man swim? asks reason. Hwȳ is assigned as a lexical adverb, not as a licence for productive instrumental syntax.

A certain man has a ship; some men have ships. Sum/mann are masculine nominative singular and scip accusative singular; sume/męnn are masculine nominative plural and scipu accusative plural. Hæfð versus habbað follows the subject.
Such men are good. Swilce is masculine nominative plural here; swilce likewise is a distinct invariant adverb. Predicative gōde agrees with męnn.

The antecedent mann is nominative singular; the first ðe is subject of hæfð. The antecedent scip is accusative singular; the second ðe is object of hæfð, whose subject is se mann. The particle does not change spelling with role. In the added sentence, ðæs is genitive masculine singular relative referring to nominative mann and expressing possession of scip. Scip remains accusative, the object of first-singular geseah; ic is its subject. The meaning is The man whose ship I saw is good.

Use the inflected relative case required inside its own clause: nominative se as subject of healp, or dative ðǣm as the person helped. The antecedent has its own main-clause case. Case attraction is an attested limited exception introduced for recognition, not an absolute requirement or assigned alternative production rule.

Translate the complete62word dialogue independently; compare the sealed private reading model and independent source-editor translation. Three men are present; the first speaker asks his companion about the third. The singular fish is one of the preceding plural fish.

Hwā is nominative in the identification question Who is the man...?; hwǣm is dative recipient in To whom do you give...?; hwilc is accusative neuter singular agreeing with the object scip in Which ship does he have? Do not force the copular identity question into an English object analysis.

Hine is accusative masculine singular, the fish. Ðǣm męnn is dative singular recipient; se is nominative masculine singular subject within the relative; mē is dative singular as the person helped. The recipient is identified as the man who helped the answering speaker.

Translate all four complete source turns using the local helps. Preserve usefulness to the listed recipients, the merchant trade sequence, absence of local production, delivery, risk, shipwreck, loss and barely escaping alive. Compare the source editor’s sealed independent witness only after solving.

Hwæt sægst ðū, mangere? asks what the merchant says. And hū? asks how he is useful in the context of his preceding claim. Mangere is supplied nominative address; no independent address paradigm is tested.

The antecedent is accusative neuter plural ðing, valuable things being bought; ðā is nominative neuter plural relative subject. Bēoð is third-person plural and ācęnnede is the supplied plural passive participle: which are not produced in this land.

He boards with cargo, rows over sea regions, sells his goods and buys valuable things not produced locally, then brings the goods here to the addressees. Risk, shipwreck and loss describe the dangers of this trading work.

Accept two of miclum plihte great risk, forlidennesse shipwreck, and lyre ealra ðinga mīnra loss of all my things, with correct meanings. Unēaðe cwic ætberstende means barely escaping alive and describes the merchant’s accompanying circumstance.

Ðæt before scip is a neuter accusative singular demonstrative determiner; ðæt before ðe is the neuter accusative singular relative pronoun, object of gesāwe. Neither occurrence is the source-only content conjunction.
